summary: The meeting focused on discussing database and file format options for storing word transcripts, annotations, alignments, and prosodic features from speech data. Participants discussed using a structured XML format (similar to NIST ATLAS or an ICSI-developed representation) versus P-files for frame-level information. Ultimately, Grad C committed to taking a closer look at the ATLAS external file representation, and participants agreed that it is worth looking at and using if suitable.

The meeting focuses on the Meeting Recorder project, specifically discussing data collection procedures, microphone usage, consenting and anonymization processes, and a proposed starter task using a belief-net to infer tourist intentions (View, Enter, or Tango mode) based on situational and linguistic features from a SmartKom-based tourist system parser output.

The team discussed data collection preparations, including the new scenario setup and tourist map creation. They reviewed the status of the parser and natural language generation modules, noting that the German generator developer produced an English version. The meeting also covered action and schema modeling for the action planner interface, specifically looking at rich action descriptions and Source-Path-Goal schemas, and rescheduled the weekly meeting time.

The meeting covered three main topics: distribution plans and potential corpus sharing with the University of Washington, transcription tools (specifically the use of Transcriber, handling of conventions, cost analysis of external transcription services versus graduate student labor, and plans for pilot testing segmentation), and electronics/hardware updates including table wiring, network cards, and cabinet design.

The meeting covered several topics including meeting procedures (such as doing digit recordings at the end), strategies for collecting meeting data and recruiting participants from groups like the Haas Business School while offering free lunch and CD-ROMs after transcripts are cleared, disk space management and archiving status, and Jose's research update on acoustic change detection, overlaps, and classification features.

The meeting primarily focused on managing and standardizing digit data and transcripts for speech recognition research. Participants discussed instructions for reading digits as single digits instead of connected numbers, speaker forms, naming conventions, disk space and scratch storage management, and transcription sanitization conventions including spell-checks, acronyms, and qualitative comments.
The meeting covered agenda items including digits performance results, forced alignment improvements, and a discussion regarding upcoming Eurospeech paper submissions and a Saturday meeting.

The meeting covered various project updates and administrative topics. The participants discussed the IBM transcription status, utilizing a new beep and digit format for file alignment, as well as the progress on transcription hours for the DARPA demo. They also addressed how to handle reading digits and whether to integrate SmartKom data into the Meeting Recorder corpus, ultimately deciding to keep SmartKom data separate due to different transcription conventions while storing it under non-backed-up disks with tape archiving. Additionally, disk storage space and the ICSI back-up system saturation were discussed, leading to a plan to use non-backed-up partitions archived via the NW archive utility. Finally, SRI recognition experiments and features were reviewed, and a brief status update on Absinthe and planning for the July DARPA demo concluded the session.

The meeting covered transcription status and plans for sending data batches to IBM, information retrieval tools and user interfaces for DARPA demos, XML tools and transcription format updates, disk backups and storage space considerations, CrossPads and potential alternative note-taking or meeting event markers (such as PDAs), and equipment/microphone wiring.

The meeting covered agenda items including transcription status, participant approval, DARPA demo status, transcriber software on Windows, and disk space issues. The team also discussed recognition results and system combinations, such as PLP configuration and Hub-five test sets, as well as future meeting focus rotation.

The meeting covered several topics, including consent forms and data release timelines for transcripts, updates on automatic transcription work and jargon terminology checks, ordering new headphones/earphones for transcribers, disk space management on the servers and incoming hardware, and preparation for a DARPA annual report phone call.

The team discusses logistics for an upcoming field trip to OGI next week, including meeting time and transportation. They also review progress reports, discussing the use of feature dimensions, training data, and testing data in a multi-dimensional setup (the 'cube'). Additionally, they talk about handling cross-language issues, phoneme mapping, and available disk space and computational resources.

The participants discussed waveform illustrations and room noise issues, including 5 Hz energy from air conditioners on PDA mics. They reviewed recent experiments on recognition rates, latency reductions, and filter effects across Italian, Spanish, and Finnish test sets. They discussed voice activity detectors (VAD), spectral subtraction challenges, and the potential use of voicing information or fine structure. Plans were made regarding Eurospeech deadlines, exploring CVS over the web, and updating website illustrations for reverberation.

The meeting covered several technical updates on HTK back-end training optimization, Linux machine setup for running experiments, Aurora conference call discussions regarding weights and baselines (including voice activity detection), feature extractions for voicing/excitation, and modulation spectrum research.

The meeting covered several technical and research topics regarding speech recognition experiments, including front-end scaling and insertion penalties, voicing detectors, training neural networks with new noise data, and acoustic events.

The participants discussed updates and issues related to the Aurora speech recognition project, including voice activity detectors, endpointing data, criteria and evaluation challenges, and alternative recognition features such as TRAPS and cepstral coefficient variance tuning. They also touched on software availability and plans to improve group communication.

The meeting involves participants discussing research progress on speech recognition features, neural nets for voice/unvoice and phoneme recognition, training data sources (like TIMIT), proposal analysis (such as France Telecom), support vector machines for phonological feature detection, and mean subtraction methods for normalizing far-field meeting audio data.

The meeting covered individual progress updates on speech enhancement and recognition work, a compute infrastructure update regarding the order of twelve new Sun Blade 100 machines and the use of P-make and Customs tools for job distribution, discussions about combining different noise removal techniques and features (such as spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering, signal subspace, and VTS), and preparations for upcoming tasks such as Wall Street Journal noisy tasks and dealing with endpoints.

The meeting involves status reports and technical discussions from participants working on speech recognition systems, proposals, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and normalization techniques. Barry discusses his upcoming proposal and qual exam in July. Dave reports on results from using mean subtraction and phase normalization approaches with SRI and HTK systems, and plans to test on a larger dataset (Macrophone). Stephane and Sunil discuss VAD problems, spectral subtraction, and Wiener filtering comparisons across datasets such as TI-digits and SpeechDat-Car Italian. Carmen discusses VTS experiments in the cepstral domain.

The participants met to discuss ongoing research and experimental results related to speech recognition and noise compensation techniques, including spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering, voice activity detection (VAD), and latency considerations.

The meeting involves participants discussing research updates on speech recognition, cepstral mean subtraction, analysis window lengths, LDA filtering, VAD (Voice Activity Detection) performance across databases like TI-Digits and SpeechDat-Car, and noise estimation issues.

The team discussed updates on their code repository, reviewed the conclusions from a mid-week meeting with Hynek regarding what to freeze in the system, evaluated their current system ranking (second place), planned for upcoming tasks including adding a second stream and improving the VAD, and discussed the upcoming Wall Street Journal evaluation task.

The meeting participants discussed progress on ASRU submissions, filter band experiments and feature sets for speech recognition, VAD latency and noise compensation, tandem neural network performance and mismatches, and scheduling for upcoming meetings.

The meeting covers updates and discussions regarding the Aurora project, including latency decisions, the use of tandem networks and silence probabilities, human performance comparisons, progress on the Wall Street Journal LVCSR task from Mississippi State, and introductory work on auditory features and Gabor functions with visiting student Michael Kleinschmidt.

The participants discussed data collection protocols for meeting recordings, including the potential use of CrossPads for importance marking, generating digital pictures of tables and boards to provide meeting context, gathering electronic minutes or summaries, and having participants mention an interesting item discussed at the end of the meeting. They also reviewed action items such as checking human subject requirements, updating web pages, setting up mailing lists, and coordinating data transfers with IBM and Picheny.

The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held its 14th meeting, conducting ministerial announcements, presenting petitions, hearing member statements on various topics including heritage months, community efforts, and international issues, and engaging in extensive questioning of ministers regarding government pandemic relief programs, N95 mask procurement, economic support, and foreign affairs.

The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic met to consider ministerial announcements, present certified petitions, and question ministers of the crown, including the Prime Minister. Topics discussed included gun control legislation, prison releases during the pandemic, China's transparency regarding COVID-19, financial support for seniors, eligibility criteria for the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB), support for farmers and agricultural producers, conditions at meat-packing plants, tax havens, support for the tourism and oil and gas industries, and military support and investigations related to the recent helicopter crash off the coast of Greece.

The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held its 15th meeting. Ministerial announcements and member statements addressed anti-black and anti-indigenous racism, the killing of George Floyd, economic relief and CERB measures, border restrictions and family reunification, agricultural and business support programs, firearms regulations, and veterans' benefits backlogs. The session also included question periods directed at various ministers concerning government actions, procurement contracts, and pandemic management.

The Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held its seventh meeting. Members presented certified petitions, questioned government ministers regarding various COVID-19 emergency programs (including CERB fraud cases, agricultural supports, student benefits, procurement, long-term care, and public safety/firearms regulations), discussed statistical leaks and government transparency, and debated jurisdictional boundaries concerning health care and provincial responsibilities.

The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held meeting number 22, during which members presented petitions on various topics including Falun Gong, the Trans Mountain pipeline, firearms laws, and COVID-19 relief. Members delivered statements on topics such as World Elder Abuse Awareness Day, systemic racism, local community heroes, and graduation accomplishments. The committee also questioned government ministers regarding economic updates, federal transfers to provinces, systemic racism in policing, the status of parliamentary proceedings, government debt, and various other public policy matters.

The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 pandemic held its sixth meeting via videoconference. Members presented various petitions from constituents regarding world maternal mental health, cystic fibrosis and Patented Medicine Prices Review Board regulations, family doctor shortages, firearms legislation, open-net salmon farming, Wet'suwet'en territory construction, and CERB-related flight refunds. During the questioning of ministers, members raised concerns regarding potential fraud flags in government benefit applications, tax evasion and avoidance conditions on large employer financing, credit card interchange and interest rates, support for single parents and the homeless, Service Canada mail delays, firearms prohibitions, CEWS and CERB repayment details, consultations on Wet'suwet'en land rights, support for seniors and procurement of personal protective equipment, seafood harvester and forestry industry supports, oil and gas sector liquidity, vaccine research models, long-term care home standards, and economic data leaks.

The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held its fifth meeting by video conference. The committee discussed petitions, questioning of ministers including the Prime Minister and various cabinet ministers, and issues related to energy workers, agriculture, fisheries, municipalities, Indigenous communities, infrastructure projects, international relations and foreign donations, justice system delays, small business support programs, tax assistance, firearms regulations, health measures, seniors' support, and testing capacities.

The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held its 12th meeting, marking its first hybrid session with members participating both in person and via videoconference. Proceedings included ministerial announcements, the presentation of various petitions (such as on national pharmacare, Bill S-204 regarding organ trafficking, and Bill C-7 regarding euthanasia safeguards), statements by members recognizing local heroes, essential workers, and community resilience during the pandemic, and a question period addressing government emergency programs (CEBA, CEWS, CECRA), conditions in long-term care facilities following a Canadian Armed Forces report, international trade and supply chains, personal protective equipment (PPE) procurement, and border restrictions.

The 13th meeting of the House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic covered committee proceedings, petitions presented by members on issues like honey bees, long-term care conditions, Bill C-7, and essential workers, as well as member statements recognizing community champions, tourism week, condolences for tragic losses, and local achievements. Ministers were questioned on topics including parliamentary virtual vs. in-person proceedings, agricultural support and calculators, energy sector financing, political party wage subsidies, senior long-term care conditions and profit models, funding for human rights and women's shelters, international human rights regarding China and Hong Kong, student employment programs, border crossing regulations and family reunification, agricultural meat processing capacity, CRA tax return processing, media sector support, airline ticket refunds, commercial rent relief, municipal financial support, and workplace safety guidelines during the pandemic.

The House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic held its 23rd meeting, during which members presented petitions on various topics such as marine protected areas, Indigenous rights, a no-fault compensation system for vaccine-injured Canadians, streaming royalty models, euthanasia, systemic racism, firearms regulations, and assistance for seniors. Members delivered statements on topics including National Indigenous Peoples Day, front-line health care workers, local celebrations, teachers, and community heroes. During the questioning of ministers, opposition members raised concerns regarding pandemic economic support programs, wage subsidies, commercial rent relief, federal spending transparency, an economic update, foreign policy, forestry sector support, high-speed Internet access in rural areas, and pandemic management. Ministers responded regarding government measures, funding allocations, and ongoing work with provinces and territories.

The meeting of the Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic involved ministerial document tablings, member petitions, and member statements concerning local community efforts, COVID-19 responses, social issues, and international affairs. This was followed by a question period directed at ministers regarding government spending, the Auditor General's budget, the CERB, financial and medical support for sectors such as tourism, agriculture, and energy, personal protective equipment, and various other domestic and international concerns.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session with the Welsh Government, featuring Minister Vaughan Gething, Deputy Minister Julie Morgan, and senior officials. Topics discussed included the impact of COVID-19 on children and young people, health services, critical care capacity, children's mental health and CAMHS services, safeguarding and child protection referrals, looked-after children and foster care, children's rights and impact assessments, and financial support for the childcare sector.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held its sixth scrutiny session on the Children (Abolition of Defence of Reasonable Punishment) (Wales) Bill, welcoming witnesses Sally Jenkins (Association of Directors of Social Services), Alastair Birch (Association of Directors of Education Wales), and Councillor Huw David (Welsh Local Government Association). Discussions focused on general support for the Bill, its clarity, implementation, potential impacts on social services and education, awareness-raising campaigns, and resource implications.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held a scrutiny session on the 'Healthy Weight: Healthy Wales' draft strategy with Dr Frank Atherton (Chief Medical Officer for Wales) and Nathan Cook (Head of the Healthy and Active Branch at Welsh Government). Discussions covered engagement with children and young people, potential obesity targets, resourcing and the sugar levy consequentials, leadership and governance structures, data and measurement (including the child measurement programme and potential second measurement points), healthy environments and planning rules, school infrastructure and sports facilities, the foundation phase and teacher training/CPD, physical education engagement, free school meals and packed lunches, the review of the clinical obesity pathway, the first 1,000 days, and socioeconomic inequalities.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session on the Welsh baccalaureate qualification with representatives from ColegauCymru and the Civil Engineering Contractors Association. Participants discussed whether employers and universities understand the Welsh bac, its level of rigor and comparability to other qualifications, student and parental perceptions, and whether it effectively prepares learners for employment.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held a scrutiny session focusing on higher and further education with Cabinet Secretary Kirsty Williams, Minister Eluned Morgan, and Huw Morris. Discussions covered teacher training and recruitment (particularly in priority subjects and Welsh-medium teaching), post-16 education and training reforms (including the Hazelkorn recommendations and the PCET Bill), equity and university widening access plans, university mergers, parity of esteem for vocational education and apprenticeships, regional skills partnerships, student mental health and well-being, FE pay disputes, and essay mills.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session on its inquiry into the impact of Brexit on higher and further education. Kirsty Williams AM (Cabinet Secretary for Education) and Eluned Morgan AM (Minister for Welsh Language and Lifelong Learning), accompanied by officials Huw Morris and Marie Knox, discussed sector preparedness, the potential impact of a 'no deal' Brexit, student recruitment and application trends, funding arrangements including ESF and ERDF, and immigration policies.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held a session with the Minister for Children and Social Care, Huw Irranca-Davies, alongside Jo-Anne Daniels and Owain Lloyd, focusing on the Welsh Government's childcare offer. Discussions covered early implementer feedback, administrative burdens, rollout plans toward 2020, workforce and capacity challenges (including Welsh-medium provision and children with complex needs), the £4.50 single national hourly rate, additional costs for parents (such as food, snacks, and transport), and comparisons with reports from PPIW regarding work outcomes.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session focusing on targeted funding to improve educational outcomes, specifically examining the pupil development grant (PDG) for free school meals, looked-after children, and adopted children, as well as lessons learned from Schools Challenge Cymru and the role of regional consortia.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee met with Estyn representatives (Meilyr Rowlands, Claire Morgan, and Simon Brown) for two evidence sessions. The first session examined targeted funding and the pupil development grant (PDG), discussing targeting towards children eligible for free school meals, support for more able and talented pupils, school leadership capacity, curriculum focus, and services for looked-after and adopted children. The second session scrutinized Estyn's annual report for 2016-17, discussing education reforms, the foundation phase, primary versus secondary school performance, post-16 education, further education colleges, work-based learning, and local authority self-evaluation.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session with the Minister for Education Kirsty Williams and Welsh Government officials regarding the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on education in Wales. Key topics discussed included the closure of all schools for statutory education starting the next day, the new operational purpose of schools to support vulnerable children and children of frontline key workers, continuity of free school meals and other support payments (such as EMA and childcare funding), the cancellation of the summer exam series and how grades will be assigned for Year 11 and Year 13 students, and the operational stance of colleges and universities.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session for its inquiry on education otherwise than at school (EOTAS). Witnesses from local authorities, the Welsh Local Government Association, Samaritans, and Mind Cymru discussed the rising number of school exclusions, challenges around additional learning needs (ALN), capacity issues in PRUs and EOTAS provision, teacher training, accountability measures, the impact of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), and mental health support for learners.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session on school improvement and raising standards, welcoming Minister for Education Kirsty Williams AM and director of education Steve Davies. The discussion covered the ongoing role of the OECD, implementation and renaming of the national evaluation and improvement resource (formerly toolkit), powers of intervention in schools causing concern, regional consortia and local government roles, performance measures, PISA targets, and closing the attainment gap for disadvantaged and minority groups.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held a scrutiny session on early childhood education and care with Deputy Minister Julie Morgan and Welsh Government officials Jo-anne Daniels and Nicola Edwards. Discussions focused on the dual objectives of supporting child development and helping parents into work, the complexity and simplification of the early years system, local authority pathfinder projects, the childcare offer, Welsh language provision, and Flying Start targeting.

The Children, Young People and Education Committee held an evidence session to scrutinise the Welsh Government's progress in developing the new curriculum for Wales. Minister for Education Kirsty Williams AM, along with officials Steve Davies and Claire Bennett, discussed feedback from the draft curriculum engagement period, plans for refining the guidance, changes to the primary legislation (including statutory provisions for 'what matters' statements and progression frameworks), feedback on religious education and relationships and sexuality education, professional learning investments, accountability frameworks, and implementation timelines targeting September 2022.

The project team met to discuss the functional design of the new TV remote control, incorporating three new company requirements: excluding teletext, restricting functionality solely to controlling the television, and including corporate colors and the slogan. Presentations were delivered by the User Interface Designer, Marketing, and the Industrial Designer. The team decided to target the 15-35 age demographic, include basic remote functions (on/off, volume up/down, channel up/down, channel numbers, and mute) with advanced features potentially hidden or grouped, stick to regular batteries instead of a rechargeable docking unit, rely on traditional infra-red transmission, and organize controls into three conceptual buckets (audio, video, and device).

The meeting is the final detailed design and evaluation meeting for the remote control project. The team reviews the prototype and discusses specifications, including the size (approximately ten centimetres in height, three and a half centimetres in width, and two point five centimetres in depth), the removal of the LCD screen and advanced chip due to cost constraints, relying instead on the TV screen to display functions via a regular chip, and using a jog-dial for volume and advanced functions. They confirm the remote will use a battery and a double-curved plastic case. Finally, they review the design evaluation criteria, discuss their satisfaction with the project's creativity, leadership, teamwork, and tools, and conclude the meeting.

The project team met to evaluate the prototype for their new remote control, discuss budget constraints, review marketing criteria, and agree on product specifications such as retaining the LCD display, using a plastic solid case, single-curved design, and a special yellow color. They also evaluated team performance and project satisfaction.

The team held their second meeting to discuss the design and requirements of a new remote control. They reviewed findings from market research, discussed physical features such as a flip-open/sea-shell design, rechargeable docking station, and touch/button layout, and noted new project requirements including limiting the control to TV only (and video), omitting teletext, incorporating corporate image/logo, and avoiding speech recognition due to cost. They also discussed ways to locate lost remotes via a base station beeper and addressed customer service and instruction manuals.

The team held a conceptual design meeting to discuss remote control properties, materials, user-interface options, and market trends. They decided on using kinetic charging with watch-type batteries, a flip-top design with an LCD display on the top side, rubberised anti-RSI buttons on the bottom side, a plastic case housing with a rubberized sleeve cover available in fruit and vegetable colors, and discussed investigating voice recognition or a whistle feature for locating the remote.

The team reviewed prototype designs and evaluated the product against market research criteria. They agreed on design features such as a plastic body with a changeable rubber outer casing, kinetic batteries, standard transmission chips, infrared placement at the front, and dual screens (an inset black-and-white touch screen on top and standard buttons on the bottom). After rating criteria like fancy look and feel, technological innovation, ease of use, fashion trends, RSI minimization, and ease of location, they concluded that the product meets specifications well enough to proceed. They discussed the budget, deciding to remove the voice recognition feature to fit within the financial target.

The team met to review marketing potential and user interface/industrial design concepts for a new television remote control. They discussed constraints from management such as the removal of teletext, keeping the design for a specific television, and incorporating corporate yellow colors and the slogan 'put the fashion in electronics'. The team voted and decided on key features for the remote control, including speech recognition, a limited number of buttons, an organic design, programmability, and a glow-in-the-dark trim.

The team discusses findings from market and user surveys regarding the remote control design, focusing on fancy outlooks, technological innovation (including speech recognition), ease of use, material feel, color choices, and power sources. They also agree to work on a clay model of the remote control for the next meeting.

The project manager introduced the design project to create an original, trendy, and user-friendly TV remote control with a production cost maximum of twelve and a half Euros to reach a profit target of fifty million Euros. Team members introduced themselves and shared their roles: Cat as Marketing Expert, Maarika as Interface Designer, Gaurav as Industrial Designer, and Jen as Project Manager. The team discussed preliminary design ideas, such as a buttonless design or menu-based interface, and noted that they will continue working individually on their respective design components before the next meeting.

The team held their final detailed design meeting for the remote control project. They presented the prototype (shaped like a banana with a rubber casing, LCD screen, and voice recognition), evaluated the design against their criteria (achieving an average score of about 6.5), reviewed production costs using an Excel spreadsheet to ensure the product was within the 12.5 budget, and provided feedback on the overall project and design process.

The team held an initial meeting for a new remote control project, covering tool training via whiteboard drawings, project financial and production constraints (including a 25 Euro selling price and 12.50 Euro production cost ceiling), and brainstorming sessions on remote control designs, ultimately leaning toward a reliable television remote with ergonomic and practical features.

The project manager and team members (Catherine for Industrial Design, Gabriel for User Interface, and Reissa for Marketing) held a meeting to present their initial work on designing a television remote control. Each member gave a brief presentation covering working design, user interface research, and marketing findings. The team decided to go with a basic television remote utilizing infrared signals and standard batteries, and discussed corporate design image and ergonomics.

The team held a detailed design meeting to review three remote control prototypes (rhombus, potato/mango, and Martian), evaluate the chosen 'potato/mango' shape against various design criteria, verify financial costs against the budget, and conduct a project process evaluation.

The team held a conceptual design meeting for a new remote control. They reviewed presentations on trend watching, interface concepts, and component design, and made several decisions regarding the remote's energy source, materials, and features.

The team held a meeting to review the remote prototype, discuss evaluation criteria, examine financial costs against the budget, and evaluate the overall project process. They confirmed prototype specifications including color, material, and single-curvature design, agreed to use a lithium battery and push-button interface, checked that costs are under the budget limit, and discussed teamwork and creativity constraints.

The team met for conceptual design, reviewing previous audience targeting and button system discussions. The Industrial Designer presented component designs involving custom cases and circuit boards, standard parts, and material options (rubber, plastic, wood, titanium). Marketing introduced current fashion and trend findings centered around a fruit and vegetable theme with a spongy feel. The User Interface designer discussed scroll-based navigation using the TV screen rather than an expensive built-in remote screen. The team discussed energy options including batteries, solar power, and dynamos, eventually favoring batteries. They concluded by agreeing to produce two prototypes and ask users for feedback.

The design group held their third meeting to discuss the new remote control. They reviewed presentations from Kate, Kendra, and Andrew covering component design, user interface, and market trends. Key determinations include using a custom-designed chip with voice recognition capabilities, incorporating a long-lasting battery source, utilizing an interchangeable case/cover for aesthetic and fashion appeal, reducing the number of manual buttons while keeping essential functions like a slider for volume and buttons for channel change and menu selection, and adopting an ergonomic shape similar to a hairbrush or a modified mouse.

The team held their second functional design meeting to discuss remote control requirements and features. The Project Manager reviewed the minutes from the first meeting. Team members gave presentations covering market research, user interface design, and technical practicalities, focusing on selling four million units with a 12.50 Euro target price. They discussed functionalities such as power, channel, and volume, along with potential features like speech recognition and rechargeable internal batteries with a docking station. Project requirements were clarified to specify a TV-only remote incorporating corporate image, colour, and slogan, while teletext is outdated and internet is coming in as important. Individual follow-up assignments were distributed for the next meeting.

This is the third meeting for the conceptual design of the remote control project. The project manager opened the meeting by reviewing the minutes from the previous session. Marketing and the designers presented their research and ideas regarding market trends, materials, energy sources, and user interfaces. The team discussed potential features such as spongy fruit-themed sleeves, titanium versus plastic or rubber casings, standard batteries versus kinetic energy, and a simplified push-button interface utilizing an on-screen TV menu rather than an embedded display screen. Towards the end of the meeting, assignments for the upcoming look and feel design, user interface design, product evaluation, and prototyping were distributed.

The project manager led a meeting to review previous minutes, examine the new remote control prototypes presented by the industrial designer and user interface designer, conduct an evaluation of the criteria and features, fill out the financial spreadsheet to ensure costs remained within the 12.5 Pound budget, and evaluate the project process.

The team discusses project requirements for a new television-only remote control, holds presentations covering research, user interface design, and marketing findings, and agrees on specific design features such as a 16-button layout, a hidden panel for detailed functions, a clap-activated tracking feature to find lost remotes, and the exclusion of teletext.

The team reviewed the prototype of the remote control, evaluated its design against criteria including appearance, innovation, ease of use, fashion elements, and corporate identity, and discussed financial and budget constraints to bring the production cost under twelve and a half Euros. Key decisions included using a plastic case instead of rubber to fit the budget while maintaining speech recognition and kinetic features, using a cherry shape for a special button, and setting the button colors. The meeting concluded with a project process and course evaluation.

The project manager, marketing expert, industrial designer, and user interface designer held their first meeting to plan the development of a new television remote control. They introduced their roles, performed a whiteboard icebreaker activity, discussed financial and market targets including a selling price of 25 euros and a maximum cost of 12.50 euros, and shared initial design ideas such as addressing button usability in the dark, adding a tracking device to prevent the remote from getting lost, and using a hidden panel for advanced functions.

The second meeting focused on presentations and discussions by the Industrial Designer, User Interface designer, and Marketing regarding the design and functional requirements of a new TV remote control. Key decisions included making the remote control a single-function television controller (excluding VCR, DVD, and internet/teletext), incorporating an alarm/buzzer system for locating the remote with an adhesive device for attachment, using lighting up buttons with a self-timed feature rather than glow-in-the-dark or voice recognition, and introducing interchangeable faceplates. Financial and environmental impacts (such as shape-memory alloys for recycling) were discussed but require further research.

The team held their third conceptual design meeting for the new remote control. They discussed research and options for internal components, energy sources, casing materials, and user interface concepts. Key decisions were made to use a kinetic energy source, a regular chip with pushbuttons, a command interface style, a plastic-and-rubber-coated casing with interchangeable face-plates, and a fruit and vegetable theme.

The team held a conceptual design meeting to review previous minutes, discuss findings from trend-watching and user interface exploration, review interior and material components, and make key decisions on the remote control's design. They decided to use basic batteries as the energy source, a plastic case with laminated rubber finger grips, and an iPod-type scroll wheel which requires a more expensive chip-on-print and an LCD screen. Toward the end, the project manager assigned follow-up work for the next meeting in thirty minutes, including interface design, look-and-feel design, product evaluation, and building a prototype.

The project manager led a meeting discussing remote control design and requirements. Anna (Marketing) presented focus group research on remote control usage habits, preferences, and demographics. Mael (Industrial Designer) presented the working design and technical components of the remote control. Matthew (User Interface) presented technical functions and future product perspectives. The team discussed potential features such as speech recognition and universal control capabilities, and ultimately decided to go for a universal type remote control for around twelve euro fifty.

The team met to discuss functional design for a remote control. They reviewed presentations on user requirements and technical design, discussed whether to include advanced features like speech recognition or LCD screens, and decided to focus on a simple television remote control featuring a channel-changing wheel and protected numeric buttons on the lower side to ensure a quick time to market.

The project manager, user interface designer, industrial designer, and marketing expert held a concept design meeting for a new remote control. They reviewed previous decisions including a simple interface, no LCD, no voice features, and a wheel to change channels. Presentations were given by the industrial designer, user interface designer, and marketing expert. They discussed trends from Paris and Milan indicating a fancy look and feel, vegetable and fruit themes, and spongy materials. Key design choices were finalized including a banana shape, a spongy box, a wheel on top, and push buttons on the sides.

The team met to discuss the functional design of a new TV remote control. They covered basic components, design constraints such as focusing on a sleek look rather than complex universal features (like controlling VCRs or DVDs), teletext inclusion, pricing, and potential features like a charging power cradle.

The team met for a conceptual design meeting regarding a new television remote control. They discussed power sources (deciding on a cradle/dock), casing materials (choosing a plastic inner shell with a rubber outer shell), user interface options (incorporating a scroll wheel for channel surfing and favorite channel programming, back-lit buttons, and a mode switch), and features such as a locator button and speaker. They rejected speech recognition and LCD screens. They also estimated a sales price bracket between 35 and 50 Euros.

The team held a functional design meeting for a new TV remote control. Presentations were given by the User Interface Designer, the Industrial Designer, and the Marketing Expert. The Project Manager introduced new product requirements, including avoiding teletext, focusing solely on television control rather than multiple home appliances, ensuring the product reflects the company image (fashion, fancy, powerful, easy to use, and yellow colour), and keeping production costs low. Participants discussed design challenges such as merging sophisticated functions with ease of use, wireless versus wired remote options, and the inclusion of fewer buttons.

The meeting focuses on conceptual design for the remote control project. The team discusses various user interface concepts (Google, fancy, and intelligent controller with speech/gesture recognition), component choices (materials like wood and plastic, LCD lighted buttons, solar energy combined with batteries, and low-level chips), and market trends (such as fruit and vegetable inspiration and spongy touch). Ultimately, the team makes decisions regarding the controller's features, materials, and components, and assigns prototyping tasks to Baba and David Jordan.

The project manager and team members hold a kick-off meeting for designing a new remote control. The team held a functional design meeting for a new remote control project. Presentations were given by the Marketing Expert, User Interface Designer, and Industrial Designer. The meeting focused on conceptual design for a remote control, covering component concepts (such as energy sources and materials), user interface features (including push buttons, LCD displays, speech recognition, and potential color or trend options like fruit and vegetable shapes/textures), and trend-watching presentations. The project manager, industrial designer, marketing representative, and user interface designer held a functional design meeting for a new television remote control. The team discusses the conceptual design meeting for a new remote control, covering component concepts such as wooden cases, advanced chips on print, power supply, and speech recognition. The team held an introductory meeting to establish roles, review project requirements and financial constraints for designing a new television remote control, and practice using the whiteboard tool. The team reviewed the minutes of the last meeting and heard presentations from the user interface designer, industrial designer, and marketing expert regarding the design and features of a new remote control. The team reviewed the minutes from the previous meeting, evaluated the prototype of the new remote control (which features a snail/oyster shape, soft rubber buttons, bright warm colors, and a voice recogniser), discussed financial costs and budget constraints, and conducted a production evaluation using a scoring scale. They discussed market research results, features such as a docking station and LCD screen, target audience considerations, and ultimately decided to focus the remote control exclusively on televisions, keep teletext with a big subtitles button, use a small LCD screen for extra button info / button explanation, and target the elderly population.

The team discusses the conceptual design, appearance, materials, and components for a new remote control targeted at a young demographic. The project manager led a conceptual design meeting where the team reviewed presentations from the industrial designer, user interface designer, and marketing representative regarding the remote control concepts. The team reviewed the remote control prototype, evaluated its design against criteria, discussed production costs and affordability, and concluded with a project and process evaluation.

The project team met to discuss remote control design and project costs, evaluated the product against user requirements using a questionnaire, and worked on the final report and product presentation.

During the functional design meeting, the Project Manager, Marketing Expert, Industrial Designer, and User Interface Designer presented findings and discussed remote control concepts. Key topics included targeting audiences under forty, maintaining a simple interface with primary buttons always accessible, incorporating an LCD/touchscreen element for secondary or extra functions, storing TV profile options in the remote's memory rather than requiring the TV to have a complex menu structure, and using a service centre or docking station for firmware updates. The team also voted on and agreed to adopt a touch screen design concept.

The project manager Martin opened the kick-off meeting for designing a new remote control. The team held a functional design meeting to discuss remote control functions, technical specifications, and marketing findings. The team held a conceptual design meeting to discuss the components, materials, user requirements, and technical features of their new remote control. The project manager, marketing representative, industrial designer, and user interface designer met for a functional design meeting regarding a new remote control. The project team met for their fourth meeting to discuss the product prototype design, evaluate the design against criteria, address budget constraints regarding the cost of components, and review the usage of tools like the SMARTboard and digital pen. The project manager led a meeting where team members (Industrial Designer, User Interface Designer, and Marketing Expert) presented their findings regarding the remote control project. The project manager, user interface designer, industrial designer, and marketing representative met to discuss the design, concepts, and components for a new remote control targeted at younger people. The project manager and team members (User Interface, Industrial Designer, and Marketing) discussed new project requirements and product concepts for a new television remote control. The team reviewed individual presentations regarding market findings, user interfaces, and technical manufacturing components for a new remote control design. They discussed casing options, energy sources, materials, and chip requirements, ultimately making several key design decisions including a single-curved rubber case, traditional batteries combined with solar power, a regular chip supporting scroll-wheels, and voice recognition.
